Basera Community Cloud: What Is a Gate Worth?

A teaching case on willingness-to-pay research, pricing and unit economics

1. Sunday night

At a quarter to eleven on the night of Sunday, 18 October 2026, Devyani Karkera was still at the dining table of her flat in Bengaluru with four windows open on her laptop and a cold cup of filter coffee beside them. In nine hours the pricing committee of Basera Community Cloud would meet, and she had asked for the meeting. As vice-president of product she had promised the board a recommendation on what to charge for Darwaza Sense, the artificial-intelligence gate module the company had spent fourteen months building.

The four windows did not agree. One held a conjoint study of 1,860 residents implying the market would bear ₹30.52 per flat per month for the full product. One held a survey of 480 resident welfare association treasurers that peaked at ₹28. One held a live price test across Indore and Coimbatore, in which the module had been sold at four prices to 240 societies and had, in aggregate, lost money. The fourth held one line from finance: the reserved GPU capacity cost ₹15.00 lakh a month whether anyone switched the module on or not.

Devyani had spent her career believing that pricing was a research problem. She was no longer certain that this one was.

2. The company, and a promise made in 2021

Basera Community Cloud was founded in Bengaluru in 2017 by Bhaskar Nadgouda, a former enterprise-software salesman, and Darsh Kulkarni, an engineer who had spent six years building video pipelines. The product was software for gated housing societies: visitor entry, maintenance billing and collection over UPI, a helpdesk, vendor and staff records, and a resident notice board. The customer was never the resident. It was the managing committee of the resident welfare association, unpaid volunteers re-elected every year who answer to an annual general meeting.

By October 2026 Basera served 12,000 societies containing 9,60,000 flats. The standard licence was ₹22 per flat per month, excluding 18 per cent GST, invoiced annually to the association and collected through NPCI-backed autopay mandates set up on Razorpay.

One decision from 2021 shaped everything that followed. In August of that year, fighting MyGate for share in Bengaluru and Hyderabad, Bhaskar had personally signed letters to 1,200 founding societies offering what the company called the Bharosa Pledge: a licence price of ₹12 per flat per month, frozen for as long as the society remained a customer. The pledge cohort held 1,20,000 flats. The reasoning was clean — land the anchor societies, upsell modules later. The letter, drafted in two days, froze "the monthly subscription price per flat" and said nothing about modules. Five years later, external counsel in Mumbai had advised that any repricing making a new module compulsory would be "materially contestable".

3. The industry

The Indian society-management market had three shapes of competitor. MyGate was the category leader and the reference price in every committee meeting. NoBrokerHood bundled gate software with its brokerage-free property platform at no separate licence fee, so in any negotiation Basera's price was compared not with ₹22 but with zero. ApnaComplex, now inside ANAROCK, sold to builder-managed townships, and ADDA held a long tail of self-managed associations. Below all of them sat register-and-pen, still the incumbent in most of the country.

Two regulatory facts pressed on the decision. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governed the visitor photographs and vehicle plates Darwaza Sense captured, and it was unresolved whether the association or Basera was the data fiduciary for that footage; Basera's contracts said processor, and no regulator had tested it. Second, maintenance charges above ₹7,500 per member per month attract GST, which made committees sensitive to anything that pushed the monthly bill upward.

Basera's exposure was not only Indian. Dinkar Pathania, the sales head in New Jersey, had spent two years selling to diaspora-owned property managers, and in March 2026 closed Barza Property Services LLC in Dubai, a 140-tower contract priced in dirhams. Its schedule carried a most-favoured-customer clause: any reduction in Basera's per-unit price in any market must reach Barza within sixty days.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Darwaza Sense entered the roadmap in August 2025. The premise was that the worst thirty seconds in any gated society is the gate itself: a guard telephoning a flat, a rider waiting, a visitor writing an illegible name in a register. Sense used camera inference to read plates, match recurring faces such as domestic staff and regular delivery partners, and pass an approval to the resident's phone before the visitor reached the barrier.

At the point of approval, the team believed three things. First, that inference would cost about ₹3.20 per flat per month, being twenty gate events per flat at ₹0.16 an event. Second, that the resident was the person who wanted the feature and would push the committee to buy it. Third, that ₹28 for the whole bundle was safe, because the March 2026 treasurer survey said so.

All three had since moved. In September 2026, after the model was retrained for night-time footage and two-wheeler plates, and after the GPU vendor repriced, finance re-estimated inference at ₹0.32 an event, or ₹6.40 per flat per month — exactly double the planning figure. The June 2026 conjoint study, run by Bela Chaturvedi from Toronto, had been recruited through the Basera resident app, which meant it measured the willingness to pay of people who do not sign the cheque. And the March survey, Devyani had discovered, went into the field three weeks after a widely reported gate-security lapse in a Gurugram township, when treasurers everywhere were being asked at the AGM why the gate register was still on paper.

The live test came last. Between 1 July and 30 September 2026, Debjani Ghoshal's team offered Sense as a paid add-on to 240 societies in Indore and Coimbatore, sixty at each of four prices. Contracts were signed and autopay mandates created: purchase, not intent. Exhibit 6 shows what happened.

5. The people

Devyani Karkera, vice-president of product, Bengaluru. She owns the recommendation and wants to price from evidence rather than from the covenant. She is not saying that she authorised the conjoint field work herself and did not read the sampling appendix until October.

Bhaskar Nadgouda, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. He wants the Series B closed and believes the product is chronically underpriced. He is not saying that he signed the 1,200 Bharosa letters personally, that several of those presidents have his mobile number, or that two have already called to ask whether the pledge holds.

Damini Vaidyanathan, chief financial officer, Mumbai. She wants gross margin protected before any module launches. She is not saying that the model she sent the lead investor in September assumed the tiered outcome in Option 2, and that a lower number will need explaining.

Darsh Kulkarni, co-founder and chief technology officer, Kolkata. He argues that Sense should ship to everyone, because an inference platform is only economic at volume. He is not saying that in July he signed a twelve-month reserved-capacity commitment of ₹1.80 crore, or ₹15.00 lakh a month, covering 2,34,375 flats and already being paid.

Bela Chaturvedi, data scientist, Toronto. She defends the conjoint as the most rigorous instrument the company has run, with a holdout hit rate of 71 per cent. She is not saying that she flagged the resident-versus-payer problem in the appendix, in one sentence, and nobody asked.

Debjani Ghoshal, head of customer success, Singapore. She ran the live test and believes it is the only honest number in the room. She is not saying that monthly society churn in the smallest segment has reached 2.1 per cent, or that she has been waiving first-quarter fees to hold accounts.

Dinkar Pathania, sales head, New Jersey. He wants one price on one page and no tiers. He is not saying that the Barza most-favoured-customer clause, which he negotiated, makes any Indian price cut expensive in dirhams.

Birva Solanki, design lead, Berlin. She argues that tiers should be named for what a society is, not for what it pays. She is not saying that she thinks Sense should be free, because it is the only feature that makes a resident open the app daily, and a daily-active resident base is what an acquirer would pay for.

8. The options as Devyani sees them

Option 1: sell Sense as an add-on at ₹9 per flat per month. This takes the live test's ₹9 cell at face value and applies its 20 per cent take-up to the whole base, giving 1,92,000 attaching flats. Add-on revenue would be ₹17.28 lakh a month against ₹12.29 lakh of inference, a contribution of ₹4.99 lakh, lifting company contribution from ₹199.20 lakh to ₹204.19 lakh. Measured instead against Darsh's ₹15.00 lakh reserved commitment, paid whether used or not, the add-on contributes ₹2.28 lakh. The pledge is untouched: it covers the licence, not a module.

Option 2: repackage into three tiers. Basera Core stays at ₹22; Basera Plus, at ₹32, adds payments, helpdesk and Sense; Basera Prime, at ₹42, adds data-protection assurance and analytics. The pledge cohort's 1,20,000 flats stay at ₹12. On Devyani's planning mix, 1,23,000 flats move to Prime, 2,74,000 to Plus and 4,43,000 stay on Core. Monthly revenue becomes ₹251.20 lakh, up ₹52.00 lakh, or 26.1 per cent. Sense would then run on 3,97,000 flats, or 41.4 per cent of the base, costing ₹25.41 lakh and leaving ₹225.79 lakh of contribution. The mix assumption is the whole argument: it implies 3,97,000 of 8,40,000 standard flats accept Sense inside a bundle, against the 20 per cent who bought it alone at ₹9.

Option 3: reprice by segment and give Sense away in the metros. Segment A standard flats go to ₹28 with Sense included; Segment B holds at ₹22; Segment C falls to ₹18 to hold ground against the free bundled competitor. Revenue becomes ₹209.20 lakh. Sense runs on all 3,60,000 Segment A flats at ₹23.04 lakh, leaving ₹186.16 lakh of contribution — ₹13.04 lakh below today. The case is defensive: Segment C is where churn runs at 2.1 per cent of societies a month.

Devyani had written the three options on a single sheet, and she distrusted the sheet. All three assume Sense is a feature to be priced. None asks whether the gate is the product and the rest of the suite the add-on, which is Birva's position and the one nobody had modelled. None separates the price a committee approves from the price a resident would pay directly, though the conjoint measured the second and the invoice collects the first. And all three take the ₹22 licence as fixed, when Exhibit 5 suggests the licence itself is the underpriced object.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The first constraint is the calendar. Almost every association contract renews on 1 April and requires ninety days' written notice of a price change, so a decision taken after 31 December 2026 cannot take effect until April 2028. Bhaskar had made it plain he would not go to the board twice.

The second is the Series B term sheet, drafted in August, which requires an annualised run rate of ₹30.00 crore by 31 March 2027. Today's is ₹23.90 crore. That means monthly revenue of ₹250.00 lakh against today's ₹199.20 lakh, a gap of ₹50.80 lakh. Only Option 2 clears it, and by ₹1.20 lakh — on a mix assumption the only live experiment the company has run contradicts.

The third is capacity. The reserved GPU block covers 2,34,375 attaching flats a month; beyond it inference bills on demand at ₹8.00 per flat-month, which would add ₹2.60 lakh to Option 2's inference cost and take it to ₹28.01 lakh. There is a hiring freeze, and the vision team in Kolkata is six engineers.

The fourth is hardware. Sense needs an edge device at each gate, at ₹14,000, and the average society has two gates. Basera charges the ₹28,000 to the association at cost. It is the largest number a treasurer sees, and it comes before any subscription revenue.

The fifth is contractual and legal. The Bharosa Pledge cannot be reinterpreted without risk; the Barza most-favoured-customer clause makes the Segment C cut in Option 3 an obligation in Dubai as well as a concession in Coimbatore; and the DPDP question of who is fiduciary for gate footage is unanswered, which matters most under Option 3, where Sense would run at every Segment A gate by default rather than by a committee's explicit choice.

10. Questions for discussion

1. What is each of Exhibits 4, 5 and 6 measuring — whose willingness, for what object, under what conditions — and what does each therefore have no right to say?

2. Exhibit 4 gives Darwaza Sense a flat-weighted willingness to pay of ₹8.27 against an inference cost of ₹6.40. What decisions does that single comparison rule in, and what does it fail to settle?

3. Exhibit 6 shows more take-up at ₹12 than Exhibit 4's Segment C part-worth allows. Which exhibit would you trust for which purpose, and how would you resolve the contradiction before 31 December?

4. The Bharosa Pledge covers 1,20,000 of the 9,60,000 flats, or 12.5 per cent, but only 7.23 per cent of revenue. Is the pledge a liability to be worked around, an asset to be used, or a commitment that simply ends the conversation?

5. Devyani suspects her own framing. Reframe the decision so that the object being priced is not the module. What research would that reframing require, and could it be finished in time?

6. It is Monday morning. What does Devyani put on one slide for the pricing committee, what does she ask the board to approve on the strength of it, and what does she tell them she does not yet know?

11. Eleven forty

Devyani closed the conjoint window and left the live test open. On the sheet beside the laptop she had written three numbers — ₹8.27, ₹6.40, ₹15.00 lakh — and beneath them the question she had not answered all weekend: whether the committee that signs the invoice and the resident who uses the gate could ever be described by one demand curve. In Kolkata the capacity clock was running. In Dubai a clause waited on a price she had not set. In Coimbatore a treasurer with 60 flats was deciding, this week, whether to keep paying at all. She put the coffee cup in the sink and did not turn off the laptop.

Willingness-to-Pay Research at Depth

The competent practitioner learns to bound a price. The expert learns that the bound is endogenous — that willingness to pay is not a property of the customer, but of a tuple the company itself largely constructs, and that most pricing research is measuring the shadow of decisions the company has already made without noticing.

This page assumes the working knowledge: that Van Westendorp bounds an acceptable range, that Gabor-Granger produces a demand curve and a revenue-maximising point, that conjoint separates the price signal from the feature signal, and that convergence across structurally different methods is worth more than any single number. It starts where that account stops — at the point where two competent practitioners, both of whom have read all of it, disagree about what to do next.

1. Two decisions, eleven weeks apart

Pune, 11 February 2026. Arvind Menon, VP of Product at Giravan Instruments, had spent the morning arguing with a spreadsheet. Giravan, founded in 2014 and now doing about ₹96 crore a year, built wireless vibration and thermal sensor nodes that clamped onto pumps, motors and gearboxes in mid-size manufacturing plants, and sold a cloud analytics subscription, Giravan Assure, that predicted bearing and misalignment failures before they took a line down. Eighty-two per cent of revenue was still hardware: ₹18,400 per node at a bill of materials of ₹7,900, plus ₹450 per node per month for the analytics. The board, at its January meeting, had set a target of 40% recurring revenue by FY28, and the only credible route was a zero-capex offer — Assure Complete — in which Giravan owned the hardware and charged a single monthly fee per node. Product marketing had proposed ₹1,250. Nobody in the room could say whether that number was brave or reckless.

The urgency was a live tender. A Pune auto-components manufacturer with four plants had asked for a quotation on 860 nodes, due 6 March, and had explicitly invited both a capex and a subscription structure. At 860 nodes the two structures differed by roughly ₹70 lakh over three years in Giravan's favour, and by considerably more than that in what they implied about who inside the customer had to sign.

Bengaluru, 24 April 2026. Sneha Bhatt, co-founder and head of product at Gitavani AI, was looking at a renewal she did not want to lose and a price she no longer believed in. Gitavani's voice agents handled inbound support and outbound collections reminders in nine Indian languages for NBFCs and consumer-durable brands. Since launch the company had charged ₹4.20 per connected minute. In May 2025 the underlying speech-recognition, model-inference and text-to-speech stack had cost ₹3.90 a minute; by April 2026 it cost ₹1.55. Gross margin had gone from 7% to 63% without a single pricing decision, which Sneha understood to be a temporary gift rather than an achievement.

Her largest customer, a Chennai-based NBFC, had come to the renewal with a proposal of its own: stop charging for minutes, charge ₹18 for each conversation the agent actually resolved. The head of collections had been clear that he would pay a premium for outcomes and nothing at all for airtime. A willingness-to-pay study Gitavani had run in October 2025 put the acceptable per-minute band at ₹3.60 to ₹5.10. By March 2026 two competitors were quoting ₹2.90. Sneha's question was not what the market would pay. It was whether a study whose shelf life was two quarters could be used to set a price with a twelve-month contract behind it.

Both decisions turn on willingness to pay, and neither is answerable by running the three standard instruments well. Arvind's problem is that the same economic value produces two different measured willingness-to-pay numbers depending on which budget line the money leaves from, and that the largest single term in his buyers' valuation is not the value of the outcome but their subjective probability that the outcome will occur. Sneha's problem is that her buyer's willingness to pay for an outcome is roughly homogeneous while her cost of producing that outcome is wildly heterogeneous, so that a single outcome price is simultaneously a 75% margin on one account and a 24% margin on another — and no willingness-to-pay instrument in the standard repertoire measures the second half of that equation. The argument of this page is that both problems are instances of one thing.

2. What the quantity actually is, and who disagrees about it

Define it precisely. The willingness to pay of a buyer for an offer is the price at which that buyer is exactly indifferent between transacting and not transacting, holding constant four things: the offer as specified, the set of alternatives the buyer perceives as available (including doing nothing), the buyer's belief about whether the offer will deliver what it promises, and the mechanism by which the money is authorised. Strip any of those four away and the number is meaningless. This is not pedantry. It is the whole of the practical difficulty, because three of those four conditioning variables are under the seller's control, which means willingness to pay is not a fact waiting to be discovered so much as an equilibrium the seller partly constructs.

The intellectual history runs along two tracks that did not meet until the 1970s. The first is economic: Alfred Marshall's consumer surplus in 1890 made the gap between what a buyer would have paid and what they did pay a formal object, and Hicks's compensating variation made it measurable in principle; William Vickrey's 1961 paper on auctions turned the reservation price into a strategic quantity that mechanisms could be designed to elicit truthfully. Becker, DeGroot and Marschak published their incentive-compatible elicitation procedure in 1964 — the respondent names a price, a random price is drawn, and they must buy if the draw is below their stated number — which remains the cleanest answer anyone has given to the problem of getting a stranger to tell the truth about money.

The second track is methodological and came out of market research and environmental economics. Peter van Westendorp's price sensitivity meter (1976) and the Gabor-Granger purchase-intent ladder (1966) were both practitioner heuristics — useful, atheoretical, and still in daily use. The formal machinery arrived through Luce and Tukey's conjoint measurement (1964), Paul Green's importation of it into marketing, Daniel McFadden's random utility model (for which he shared the 2000 Nobel), and Louviere and Woodworth's 1983 formulation of discrete choice experiments, which is what everybody now means when they say conjoint. In parallel, environmental economists spent three decades on contingent valuation — asking people what they would pay to prevent an oil spill — and produced the field's most brutal literature on hypothetical bias, culminating in the 1993 NOAA panel chaired by Kenneth Arrow and Robert Solow, which concluded that stated-preference numbers were admissible as evidence only under a long list of design conditions that almost no commercial pricing study satisfies.

Out of that history come five positions that are genuinely held by serious people and genuinely incompatible. It is worth stating what each will and will not sign, because a product leader refereeing a pricing argument is usually refereeing a collision between two of them that neither party has named.

The stated-preference school — the Sawtooth tradition, Richard Johnson, Bryan Orme, the people who run the conjoint. Will sign: a well-designed choice experiment recovers relative trade-offs, feature-to-feature and feature-to-price, accurately enough to design a package and set a price ladder. Will not sign: the absolute level it produces is a forecast of demand. Their own validation literature, based on holdout tasks, shows good rank-order and share prediction and systematic level error, and they say so.

The revealed-preference school — experimentalists, growth teams, the economists who run geo-holdout tests. Will sign: the only credible willingness-to-pay estimate is one produced by a real buyer facing a real price with real money. Will not sign: a survey number should ever set a launch price. Their evidence is the repeated, replicable gap between stated intent and observed conversion, and the fact that a live price test costs less than a conjoint study in most digital businesses.

The incentive-compatible school — descendants of Becker-DeGroot-Marschak, and in marketing, Min Ding's incentive-aligned conjoint. Will sign: hypothetical bias is a design defect, not a law of nature; put real money at risk inside the instrument and the bias largely disappears. Will not sign: you need a live market to get an unbiased number. Ding's 2007 experiments, in which respondents actually had to buy the profile they chose, cut the overestimate sharply. The objection is practical: you cannot put a ₹22 lakh industrial subscription into a BDM lottery.

The economic-value school — Thomas Nagle, Kent Monroe, Hermann Simon, and every value-based pricing consultancy since. Will sign: willingness to pay is bounded above by the quantified economic value of the next best alternative plus the monetised differentiation, and you should compute that ceiling from the buyer's own operations rather than ask the buyer how they feel. Will not sign: the customer's stated number is the primary evidence. Their strongest case is B2B, where the buyer often cannot articulate a value they can nonetheless verify on their own production data.

The constructed-preference school — behavioural: Ariely, Loewenstein and Prelec's 2003 "coherent arbitrariness" experiments, in which subjects' bids for consumer goods were dragged around by the last two digits of their national identity number, yet remained perfectly ordered within the category. Will sign: there is no stable latent reservation price; there is a construction process, and the instrument is part of it. Will not sign: a measured willingness-to-pay distribution describes something that existed before you measured it.

The five are not reconcilable by synthesis, and the honest thing is to notice which one a given recommendation is standing on. The position taken here — and it is a position, not a consensus — is closest to the constructed-preference school in its diagnosis and closest to the economic-value school in its prescription: because the number is partly manufactured, the highest-leverage work is not measuring it more precisely but changing the conditions that generate it.

3. Mechanics, worked through

The distribution is the object; the demand curve is its shadow

The first thing an expert does with willingness-to-pay data that a competent practitioner does not is refuse to collapse it. A willingness-to-pay study produces, for a defined population, a distribution over reservation prices. The demand curve is simply the survival function of that distribution: the share of the population whose reservation price is at or above p. Everything downstream — revenue curve, profit curve, optimal price, the argument for a second tier — is arithmetic on that one object. Report a mean and you have thrown away the only part that matters, because the mean tells you nothing about whether the distribution is tight (one price captures nearly everyone, tiering is a waste of effort) or bimodal (one price is guaranteed to be wrong for both modes).

Giravan's study, run in January 2026 by an independent firm, Gitansh Research Partners, screened to 100 plant-level economic buyers and produced the distribution in the left panel below. Table 1 does the arithmetic the survey vendor did not.

Figure 1. Giravan Assure Complete, January 2026. The histogram on the left and the demand curve on the right are the same data: the curve is the histogram's survival function. Note that the revenue-maximising price (₹1,000) and the profit-maximising price (₹1,200) are two grid points apart, and that the profit curve is almost flat between them — the decision is far less precise than the arithmetic looks.

Three things in this table deserve attention that they rarely get. First, the revenue-maximising price and the profit-maximising price are not the same, and the gap is entirely a function of variable cost: at zero cost to serve they coincide, and as cost to serve rises the profit optimum moves up the price axis and the volume optimum moves down. A Gabor-Granger revenue index — the calculation most pricing decks stop at — silently assumes a zero-marginal-cost business, which is false for anyone shipping hardware and increasingly false for anyone shipping inference.

Second, the formal condition is worth stating because it disciplines the argument. At the profit-maximising price the Lerner condition holds: the contribution margin as a fraction of price equals the reciprocal of the absolute price elasticity, (p − c)/p = 1/|ε|. At ₹1,200 the contribution margin is 990/1200 = 82.5%, which requires an elasticity of −1.21. The midpoint arc elasticity measured against the next lower grid point is −1.19; against the next higher point it is −2.42. The true optimum is therefore bracketed but not located, and with an eight-point grid that is as tight as the arithmetic gets. An expert says "somewhere between ₹1,150 and ₹1,300, and the curve is flat enough that the choice within that range should be made on grounds other than this study" — which is precisely the sentence the vendor's report did not contain.

Third, and most consequentially, the flatness of the profit curve between ₹1,000 and ₹1,400 — ₹687, ₹693, ₹571, a spread of under 5% at the top — means the study cannot adjudicate Giravan's actual question. Over that range the profit difference is smaller than the error on the estimate. The decision has to be made on something the study does not measure: the effect of the price on the sales cycle, on the discount the field will subsequently demand, and on what the number signals about the product's seriousness.

Conjoint: the ratio problem, and why the confidence interval is the finding

In a discrete choice experiment the analyst estimates a utility function, typically U = βprice·p + Σ βkxk + ε, and converts a feature part-worth into money by dividing: the willingness to pay for feature k is βk / (−βprice). This step, performed routinely and reported as a rupee figure to the nearest ten, is statistically treacherous. It is a ratio of two estimated coefficients, each with its own standard error. The distribution of such a ratio is heavy-tailed — in the limiting case of two independent normals it is Cauchy, which has no finite mean — and the practical consequence is that as the price coefficient's standard error grows relative to its magnitude, the implied willingness-to-pay distribution develops a tail so fat that the sample mean becomes unstable and sometimes meaningless. This is why careful analysts report the median, why Kenneth Train and Melvyn Weeks proposed estimating directly in "WTP space" (reparameterising so the money quantity is the estimated parameter and inherits a sane prior), and why the single best question to ask a research vendor is not "what is the willingness to pay for this feature" but "what is the 80% interval around it." If the answer is a point estimate, the study has not been analysed, only run.

Two further pieces of machinery separate a serious conjoint from a ritual one. The first is design efficiency: the choice tasks must be constructed so that attribute levels are balanced, roughly orthogonal, and sufficient in number. Johnson and Orme's rule of thumb — respondents ≥ 500 × (largest number of levels on any attribute) ÷ (tasks × alternatives per task) — is crude but catches the common disaster of a fourteen-attribute design fielded to ninety people. The second is heterogeneity: hierarchical Bayes estimation recovers individual-level part-worths rather than a single population average, and this matters more than it sounds, because the pricing question is never "what does the average buyer value" but "how much of the value sits above the price I am contemplating." A population with a mean willingness to pay of ₹1,200 and no variance is a one-price market; the same mean with a standard deviation of ₹450 is a three-tier market, and the difference is invisible in any report that leads with an average.

The calibration step almost nobody budgets for

A market simulator built from conjoint part-worths will happily predict shares for any price and bundle you feed it. The discipline that distinguishes a usable simulator from a fiction is the base case: feed it today's actual products at today's actual prices and check whether it reproduces today's actual market shares. It almost never does on the first pass, because the model omits brand, incumbency, distribution and the sheer inertia of installed systems. The fix is an external effect adjustment — tuning alternative-specific constants until the simulator reproduces observed reality — after which the simulator's differences can be trusted even though its levels could not. Skipping this step is the single most common reason a conjoint-derived price underperforms in market, and it is skipped because it requires reliable share data that the commissioning team often does not have and does not want to admit it does not have.

Weighting: the respondent is not the unit of value

Gitansh's first cut of the Giravan data gave every one of the 100 plants one vote. But Giravan does not sell to plants; it sells to nodes. The plants in the top two willingness-to-pay buckets averaged 340 nodes each; those in the bottom two averaged 45. Re-weighting the survival function by node count moved the profit optimum from ₹1,200 to ₹1,340, because the plants willing to pay more were also the plants with more to buy. This is not a subtlety; it is a 12% revision to the answer, produced by a step no standard template includes. The general rule: willingness to pay must be weighted by the quantity of the value metric each respondent commands, and in any market where account size varies by an order of magnitude, an unweighted study is simply wrong.

5. Hard edge cases

Hardware plus software: the same rupees, two different answers

Giravan's study asked the capex question and the opex question of the same 100 people, separated by enough intervening material that most respondents did not connect them. The capex structure was ₹18,400 per node plus ₹450 a month; the opex structure was ₹1,250 a month and nothing upfront. Over 36 months, at a 14% annual discount rate, the capex structure costs the buyer ₹18,400 + ₹450 × 29.26 = ₹31,570 in present value per node; the opex structure costs ₹1,250 × 29.26 = ₹36,575. The subscription is 16% more expensive in present value, and on Giravan's side it is worth about ₹5,000 more per node in present-value contribution after funding the ₹7,900 bill of materials at t=0. Yet 61 of the 100 respondents preferred the subscription, and the median stated willingness to pay under the subscription structure implied a higher total outlay than the same respondents would sanction as capex.

The explanation is institutional, not psychological. In a mid-size Indian manufacturing company, an ₹18,400-per-node capital purchase across 200 nodes is a ₹36.8 lakh capital appropriation requiring a payback calculation against a two-year hurdle and, in most promoter-run firms, a signature well above the plant head. A ₹1,250-per-node monthly charge across the same 200 nodes is ₹30 lakh a year of maintenance opex, which at many of these firms the plant head can authorise within an annual budget already approved in aggregate. The same economic value produces a different willingness to pay because it lands on a different budget line with a different signatory and a different approval calendar. An expert designs the instrument to measure this deliberately — same value, two accounting treatments, randomised order — rather than discovering it accidentally.

The credibility coefficient, and why it is the biggest term

Set the survey aside and compute the economic value from the buyer's operations, the way the value-based school would. Figure 2 does this per node per year.

The differentiation value — ₹11,600 of avoided unplanned stoppage (0.29 avoided events per machine-year × 4.2 hours × ₹9,500 per hour of lost contribution) plus ₹2,800 of avoided secondary damage — is multiplied by 0.55, the probability plant engineers assigned to the model actually catching a given failure. The arithmetic matters less than its shape. Of the ₹14,400 of gross value on the table, the belief discount removes ₹6,480 — more than the incumbent contract is worth in total. If Giravan can move plant engineers' subjective catch probability from 0.55 to 0.75, the economic value ceiling rises from ₹10,420 to ₹13,300 per node per year, an improvement of ₹2,880 that no price change and no feature can produce. And a product team can move it: by publishing per-failure-mode recall from the installed base, by running a paid three-month proof on the customer's own worst two machines, by offering a shared-savings clause, by warranting a refund of twelve months' fees for any catastrophic failure the model missed with a detectable precursor. Each of these is a product and contract decision, not a pricing decision, and each raises measured willingness to pay by more than any refinement of the survey instrument would.

This is the page's central claim in its sharpest form. Willingness to pay decomposes, roughly, into reference value, differentiation value, credibility, and budget mechanism. Reference value is set by competitors. The other three are set by the seller. A team that spends six weeks measuring the resulting number more precisely, and no time on the three terms it controls, has mistaken a thermometer for a thermostat.

Two-sided: the joint surface

Giriraj Freight Exchange, a Gurugram intercity trucking marketplace with about 14,000 registered fleet owners, ran a shipper-side conjoint in late 2025 on a proposed guaranteed-placement service level and found that shippers would accept a take rate of 11%, up from 8%, on an average Delhi–Nagpur load of ₹42,000 — worth ₹1,260 more per load. The finding was real and the resulting price increase was a failure, because a parallel study Giriraj had not commissioned would have shown that at 11% the top-quartile fleet owners, who supplied 41% of capacity, began settling off-platform with shippers they had already met through it. Willingness to pay in a two-sided market is a surface over two prices, not a point on one, and the binding constraint is almost always the side with the cheaper outside option. The methodological implication is uncomfortable: the correct instrument is a joint design in which the seller-side reservation discount and the buyer-side willingness to pay are estimated together, and nearly nobody runs one, because it doubles the cost and each side is owned by a different general manager.

Regulated markets: public procurement publishes the reference price

Giritara Diagnostics, a Hyderabad manufacturer of point-of-care HbA1c analysers, sells instruments cheaply and earns on cartridges. A 2025 study among private pathology labs put median willingness to pay at ₹128 per test. In the following year a southern state health department awarded a public tender at ₹61 per test, and the award — as all such awards are — was published. Within two quarters, median willingness to pay among the same private labs had collapsed to ₹78. Nothing about the value of the test had changed; a reference price had been created and made public. In India, public procurement through state health departments and the Government e-Marketplace is the single largest publisher of reference prices in several categories, and pricing regimes such as the NPPA's ceilings on notified devices create visible anchors that spill far beyond the products they cover. A willingness-to-pay study run before a tender award and used after it is not stale; it is measuring a market that no longer exists.

The organisational seam: list price versus realisation

Here is what mature companies actually do, as distinct from what their pricing pages imply. They run conjoint, they set a list price, and then the discount authority matrix does the real pricing. In most enterprise software businesses the realised average selling price sits at 55–75% of list, and the variance across deals of similar size is larger than the variance the conjoint was trying to resolve. A willingness-to-pay study conducted on list price in such a company is measuring a fiction unless the instrument shows respondents the prices they would actually be quoted. The mature response is not to abolish discounting but to instrument it: a standing realisation dashboard by segment and rep, a quarterly review of the discount distribution's right tail, and a rule that any repricing exercise begins with the realisation data and only then commissions primary research. Companies that skip this step reprice their list, watch their realisation absorb the change within two quarters, and conclude that pricing research does not work.

6. Ten things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

1. They ask for the distribution, never the average

A competent practitioner asks what customers will pay; an expert asks what the seventieth percentile will pay, and what the histogram looks like below it. The reason is that pricing decisions are decisions about which part of a distribution to serve, and the mean is the one statistic that answers no such question. The tell-tale sign in the wild is a pricing deck whose central exhibit is a single number with a plus-or-minus attached: that formatting is only possible if someone has already collapsed the object they needed. The obvious reading — that the average is a reasonable summary — is wrong because willingness-to-pay distributions in B2B are routinely right-skewed by a handful of very large accounts, so the mean sits above the median and below the point where the money is.

2. They weight respondents by the value metric, not by headcount

One respondent, one vote is the correct rule for elections and the wrong rule for pricing. The Giravan re-weighting moved the optimum by 12% for the simple reason that willingness to pay correlated with plant size. The tell is that an expert's first question about a sample is not "how many" but "how many nodes, seats, beds, or transactions do these respondents collectively represent, and how does that compare with the actual market." Where the correlation between size and willingness to pay is positive, unweighted studies understate the optimal price; where it is negative — often true in markets where large buyers have procurement departments and small buyers do not — they overstate it. Either way the error is systematic, not random, so more sample does not fix it.

3. They treat the choice set as part of the measurement, not the background

What a respondent is willing to pay depends entirely on what else was on the screen. A conjoint in which the company's own existing product does not appear will measure willingness to pay for the new product as though the new product were the only way to get any of the value — which converts cannibalisation into apparent incremental demand. Similarly, a study whose "none of these" option is a bare checkbox rather than a described status quo ("continue with your current quarterly manual inspection contract at ₹3,900 per machine per year") systematically overstates adoption. The tell: an expert asks to see the actual choice card before they will discuss the result, and looks first at the none-option and the competitor rows.

4. They know that a WTP figure is a ratio of two noisy estimates

The conversion of a part-worth into rupees divides one estimated coefficient by another, and the resulting statistic is far less stable than the underlying model. An expert recognises this in the wild by the absence of an interval: if a report says "customers will pay ₹340 more for real-time alerting" and cannot say whether the 80% interval is ₹280–₹400 or ₹90–₹900, the analyst has not examined their own output. The obvious reading — that a well-fitting model gives a well-determined willingness to pay — is wrong because the fit of the choice model and the precision of the price coefficient are different things, and a model can predict choices well while pinning down the money conversion badly.

5. They ask what the tested price range was before they ask what the answer was

Anchoring in pricing instruments is not a minor bias; it is the mechanism by which a great deal of the answer is produced. The coherent-arbitrariness result — that absolute valuations move with arbitrary anchors while relative valuations stay stable — has a direct operational reading: trust a study's rank-orderings and trade-offs, distrust its levels. The tell-tale sign is a study whose optimal price lands suspiciously near the centre of the tested grid, which is where anchoring puts it when respondents have weak priors. An expert asks for the grid first, and if the estimate sits at an edge, treats it as censored rather than measured.

6. They settle the value metric before they measure the level

"What should we charge" is a question with no meaning until "what are we charging for" has been answered, and the second question is usually worth ten times the first. Gitavani's real decision is between minutes, resolved conversations and a platform fee; each implies a different distribution of volume risk, a different cost exposure, and a different relationship between customer success and Gitavani's revenue. An expert recognises a premature level study by its attribute list: if the pricing attribute has one metric and four levels rather than three metrics, the team has assumed away its own decision. The cost of getting this wrong is not a suboptimal price but a business model that fights its own customers.

7. They ask which budget line the money comes from

Two offers of identical present value can differ by 30% in measured willingness to pay purely because one is capital and one is operating expenditure, or because one falls inside a budget already approved and the other requires a fresh appropriation. In Indian mid-market manufacturing the difference is often decisive; in enterprise software the equivalent is whether the spend can be routed through an existing master services agreement. The tell: an expert's discovery questions include "who signs this, out of which budget, and when was that budget set" — three questions that appear in no willingness-to-pay template and predict close rates better than the price does.

8. They separate willingness to pay from willingness to switch

A buyer may value your product at ₹1,400 a month and value the incumbent at ₹1,100, and still not move, because migration costs them ₹9 lakh of integration and three months of risk. The relevant quantity for a challenger is willingness to pay net of switching cost amortised over the expected contract life, and it can be negative for buyers who genuinely prefer the product. The tell-tale sign is a study with strong preference scores and a stalled pipeline: the standard reading is that sales is underperforming; the expert reading is that the instrument measured preference in a world without migration and the market is not that world. The corrective is to put switching cost into the conjoint as an attribute with real levels, which almost nobody does because it is unflattering.

9. They know the pitch partly creates the willingness to pay it measures

Respondents in a concept test are reacting to a description someone wrote. Change "predicts equipment failures" to "gives your maintenance team eleven days' warning on bearing failure, validated across 4,200 machine-years", and the measured willingness to pay moves — not because the product changed but because the credibility term did. The tell: an expert asks to read the concept statement and the stimulus material before reading the numbers, and treats a study run before the value story exists as a measurement of the value story's absence. The uncomfortable corollary is that a study cannot be run "neutrally": every framing is a framing, and the only honest posture is to disclose the one used.

10. They treat convergence sceptically when the methods share a sample and a grid

The standard advice — that agreement between structurally different methods is stronger evidence than any single method — is correct in principle and routinely misapplied. If the same respondents see the same price grid in a Van Westendorp block and then a Gabor-Granger block twenty minutes later, the second instrument inherits the first one's anchors, and the convergence is contamination rather than corroboration. Genuine triangulation requires either independent samples or independent price grids, and ideally a method whose data-generating process is different in kind — a live test, a pilot, an observed win-loss curve. The tell: an expert asks whether the methods were fielded to the same people in the same session, and discounts the convergence accordingly if they were.

7. What changes by product type and company stage, and what does not

Begin with what does not change, because the differences are usually overstated. The random utility model underlying conjoint is identical whether the product is a face serum or a turbine monitoring subscription. The ratio problem is identical. The need for base-case calibration is identical. The fact that stated intent overstates behaviour is identical in direction if not in magnitude. Practitioners who insist that "B2B pricing research is completely different" are usually describing differences in sample construction and stakeholder structure, not in method.

What genuinely differs is this. In consumer markets, samples are large and cheap, the buyer and user are the same person, and the binding constraint is the competitive shelf: an instrument that does not show real competitor products at real prices is not measuring anything a shopper would recognise. In B2B mid-market, samples are small enough that individual-level estimation is marginal and the dominant error source is which single person in the account answered. In enterprise, the buying committee makes the individual respondent the wrong unit entirely — the relevant construct is the committee's joint reservation price, which is closer to the minimum across veto-holders than to any average, and the practical substitute is win-loss price analysis on the company's own closed deals, which is revealed preference and free. In platforms and marketplaces, willingness to pay is a surface over both sides and the price object is usually a take rate or a fee structure rather than a level. In hardware, the capex approval path and the depreciation schedule are first-order determinants, and residual value and financing availability enter the buyer's calculation in ways no software study contemplates. In AI-native products, the two live differences are that cost to serve is stochastic and account-specific, and that the reference price is set by a rapidly falling model-API price that the buyer can look up.

Stage matters in a simpler way than is usually claimed. Before product-market fit, formal willingness-to-pay research is close to malpractice, not because the methods fail but because condition C1 fails: there is no stable offer to price, and the cheapest instrument available — quoting a real number to a real prospect and watching their face — has a faster cycle time and better information content than any survey. In the growth stage, the highest-value use is packaging: conjoint to determine which features belong in which tier and what the fences should be, with the level almost a by-product. At scale, with a large installed base, the acquisition price becomes the least interesting price: renewal uplift, expansion pricing and the discount matrix move more money, and the appropriate instrument shifts from surveys to controlled live tests on new-prospect cohorts. Giravan is a growth-stage company with a structure problem; Gitavani is an early-scale company with a value-metric problem; neither has a level problem, which is what both of them initially thought they had.

If Gitavani prices minutes, it is selling a commodity whose cost curve is visible to everyone. If it prices resolved conversations, or recovered rupees, the reference price is a human collections agent at ₹38 a conversation, and that number is going up, not down.

9. Failure modes, with their early warnings

Pricing the list while selling the discount. Early warning: realisation — average selling price divided by list — drifts down quarter over quarter while win rates stay flat. Diagnostic question: what is our realised ASP as a percentage of list, by segment and by rep, and how has it moved in six quarters? Cost of catching it late: an entire repricing exercise whose effect is absorbed by the discount matrix within two quarters, plus the credibility cost of having told the board it would work.

The uncalibrated simulator. Early warning: the conjoint simulator, fed today's real products at today's real prices, predicts shares materially different from actual. Diagnostic question: what does the base case produce, and what external effect adjustment was applied? Cost of catching it late: a launch forecast that is wrong by a factor rather than a margin, and a planning cycle built on it.

Attributes the buyer cannot perceive. Early warning: a part-worth that is flat across its levels, or an attribute where the "importance" score is high but sales has never heard a customer mention it. Diagnostic question: could a buyer detect the difference between these two levels in a twenty-minute demo, without being told which they were seeing? Cost of catching it late: a roadmap prioritised by a study that measured engineering's vocabulary rather than customer preference.

Invisible cannibalisation. Early warning: the simulator's predicted share for the new offer exceeds the sum of plausible competitor losses plus category growth. Diagnostic question: was our own current product in the choice set, at its actual price, with its actual terms? Cost of catching it late: a new tier that grows in units and shrinks total revenue, discovered two quarters after launch when the mix shift shows up in ARPU.

Level before metric. Early warning: the pricing attribute in the study has exactly one unit of measure. Diagnostic question: what are the three candidate things we could charge for, and which of them correlates best with both the customer's value and our cost? Cost of catching it late: a year of contracts written on the wrong metric and a migration that requires renegotiating every one of them.

One persona, many signatories. Early warning: the study's respondents all hold the same job title. Diagnostic question: in the last ten closed-won deals, how many people had to agree, and who could have said no? Cost of catching it late: a price that clears the champion's enthusiasm and dies in procurement, showing up as lengthening cycles rather than lost deals, which is a much harder signal to read.

Pricing at the measured ceiling. Early warning: win rates hold but the sales cycle lengthens by 20% or more, and the proportion of deals requiring an exception approval climbs. Diagnostic question: what have we left for the negotiation, and what happens to our credibility when we concede it? Cost of catching it late: the discount becomes the expected behaviour, and the list price stops carrying information for anybody.

Re-running the study until it agrees. Early warning: a second study commissioned within six months of the first, with a changed concept statement. Diagnostic question: what decision rule did we write down before the first study, and are we now changing the evidence or the rule? Cost of catching it late: the organisation learns that research is a rhetorical instrument, and stops funding the kind that would have been useful.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether stated preference can set an absolute level. The experimentalist position, in its strongest form: every controlled comparison we have between stated intent and observed behaviour shows a gap, the gap is large, it varies by category and by instrument in ways nobody can predict in advance, and there exists no published deflator that reliably converts one into the other. Therefore survey output is admissible for ranking and inadmissible for levels. The stated-preference position, in its strongest form: holdout validation in thousands of commercial conjoint studies shows good share prediction once the simulator is calibrated, the calibration step is exactly the correction the experimentalists are demanding, and refusing to use surveys means most companies will price on management intuition, which is worse than a biased instrument with a known bias direction. What would have to be true for the experimentalists to be wrong: a stable, published, cross-category deflator between stated and revealed willingness to pay. What would have to be true for the survey school to be wrong: evidence that calibrated simulators fail out of sample as badly as raw ones. Neither exists.

Whether a latent reservation price exists at all. The constructed-preference position rests on experiments in which arbitrary anchors move absolute valuations while leaving relative valuations intact — a result replicated enough to be taken seriously. The realist position rests on the observation that price elasticities in mature, frequently purchased categories are stable across decades and across countries, which is hard to reconcile with valuations being freshly invented at each encounter. The reconciliation people reach for — that preferences are constructed for novel goods and retrieved for familiar ones — is plausible and largely untested, and it has an awkward implication for product managers: the goods we most want to price are exactly the novel ones, where the construction story applies. If the constructionists are right, the seller's job is partly to build the reference frame, which sounds like manipulation and is in fact just marketing, and the honest version of it is to build the frame around evidence the buyer can verify.

Value ceilings versus customer statements. Giravan's case is the disagreement in miniature. The economic-value calculation puts the ceiling at ₹10,420 per node per year. The survey puts the median stated willingness to pay at ₹14,400. The value school reads the gap as proof of hypothetical bias and would price under ₹10,420. The survey school reads it as proof that the value model omits real value — reputational risk, the operations head's personal exposure when a line stops during a customer audit, the optionality of the data itself — and would price near ₹14,400. Both readings are coherent, and the evidence that would separate them is a live test that neither side is proposing to run because the tender is in three weeks. What would have to be true for the value school to be wrong: buyers consistently paying above computed ceilings in repeat purchases, not just in first purchases where enthusiasm is highest. That evidence exists in some categories and not others.

Whether pre-fit companies should price research at all. The "just charge and see" position is stronger than it sounds: the fastest unbiased willingness-to-pay instrument in existence is an invoice, an early-stage company has few enough prospects that every one can be a test, and the information from one real signature dominates fifty survey responses. The counter-position is about irreversibility: in enterprise and regulated markets a published price anchors the category and a customer who signed at ₹X will not accept 2₹X at renewal, so the cost of a wrong early price is paid for years. Both are right in their own domains, and the discriminating variable is how reversible the price is, which is a function of contract length, market visibility and whether prices are published.

Whether AI makes the discipline more or less valuable. One camp holds that in a category where the input cost falls 60% a year and capability jumps every quarter, no willingness-to-pay study survives its own analysis phase, and the correct posture is continuous live testing with short contracts. The other holds the opposite: precisely because there is no reference price for an autonomous agent that resolves a collections call, structured research is the only way to find out what buyers are comparing it to, and the answer — a human agent, an IVR licence, a competitor's per-minute quote — determines the entire pricing strategy. Sneha holds both views on different days, which is the appropriate response to a genuinely open question.

And one thing on which there is simply no settled answer: how much to discount stated intent. The folk deflators in circulation — halve the "definitely would buy" and take a fifth of the "probably" — have no general empirical basis. Each firm's deflator is idiosyncratic, discoverable only by running studies, launching, and recording the ratio. The firms that know theirs are the ones that kept records. Almost nobody keeps records.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in four visible ways. First, they write the decision rule before the data arrives: "if the node-weighted seventieth percentile is above ₹1,300 we launch Assure Complete at ₹1,250 and drop the capex option from the tender; if it is below ₹1,100 we quote capex and revisit in FY28." This costs an hour and eliminates the single largest source of research waste, which is the retrofitting of conclusions.

Second, they spend their effort on the terms they control. Faced with a ₹6,480 credibility discount, they commission a proof on the customer's worst machines rather than a second wave of the survey, because the first raises the ceiling and the second only measures it. Third, they keep a pricing memory: a running record of every study's prediction, the price actually set, and the outcome observed, so that the firm's own deflator becomes knowable after four or five cycles rather than remaining folklore forever. Fourth, and most tellingly, they refuse to supply a single number when asked for one, and instead supply a range, the decision the range supports, and the specific observation that would change it. The competent practitioner produces a price. The expert produces a price, an expiry date, and a tripwire.

12. What Arvind and Sneha decided

Arvind quoted the Pune tender at ₹1,150 per node per month on the subscription structure and did not quote a capex alternative, on the reasoning that the profit curve between ₹1,150 and ₹1,340 was flat enough that the ₹190 he gave up was cheap insurance against a longer procurement cycle, and that offering both structures would route the decision to the capital-appropriation committee and add a quarter. He attached two things the pricing study had not asked about: a published recall figure by failure mode from Giravan's installed base, and a clause refunding twelve months of fees on any catastrophic failure that the system missed with a detectable precursor in the data. Internally he described the clause not as a concession but as the cheapest available purchase of ₹2,880 per node per year of credibility. He also set a review for September 2026 to re-estimate the distribution node-weighted, having conceded that the January study's unweighted sample had understated the optimum by roughly 12%.

Sneha did not accept the NBFC's ₹18 per resolved conversation, and did not counter with ₹24.50 either. She proposed a two-part tariff: a platform fee of ₹1.4 lakh a month covering the first 8,000 attempted conversations, plus ₹16 per resolved conversation beyond that, with a data-quality threshold written into the contract — if the customer's contactable-number rate fell below 60%, the resolved- conversation rate reverted to ₹22. The structure priced the part of the value the customer wanted to buy (outcomes) while keeping the part of the cost the customer controlled (data quality) on the customer's side of the line. She also stopped quoting per minute to new prospects entirely, on the grounds that a metric whose reference price was a publicly posted and rapidly falling model-API rate was a metric she would be defending forever. The October 2025 study went into the archive with a note on the front page recording the date it stopped being true.

Discussion questions.

1. Giravan's economic-value calculation and its willingness-to-pay survey differ by ₹3,980 per node per year. Which number should Arvind have taken to the tender, and what single piece of evidence — not another survey — would have settled the question inside three weeks?

2. Gitavani's per-minute pricing produces an identical 63.1% gross margin on its best and worst accounts, while outcome pricing produces 75% and 24%. Under what circumstances is the volatile metric nonetheless the right choice, and what would Gitavani have to be able to measure before signing a contract for that choice to be defensible?

3. Gitika Naturals' Van Westendorp study was executed competently and produced a number that was useless. If a study can be methodologically sound and decision-destroying at the same time, what should a product leader require of a research brief before it is commissioned — and who inside the company should have the authority to refuse one?

13. Going deeper

  1. Willingness-to-pay probes in interviews. The qualitative ancestor of everything here; worth revisiting because a well-run probe surfaces the reference set and the budget mechanism, which are the two conditioning variables the formal instruments assume rather than measure.
  2. Conjoint and MaxDiff. The formal machinery in detail — design efficiency, hierarchical Bayes, simulator calibration — and MaxDiff for the prior question of which attributes even belong in the study.
  3. Price testing. The revealed-preference answer to everything this page left unresolved: how to run a live price experiment that is statistically valid, commercially survivable and defensible to customers who compare notes.
  4. When to charge. Timing interacts with willingness to pay directly — measured WTP at first contact, after a pilot, and at renewal are three different distributions for the same buyer.
  5. The value metric. Established here as the decision that dominates the level; the topic itself works through how to choose a metric that correlates with customer value and with your own cost to serve, which Table 3 shows are not the same requirement.
  6. Packaging: good / better / best. What you do with a heterogeneous WTP distribution: tier design, fencing and the arithmetic of how much a middle tier cannibalises versus expands.
  7. Freemium vs free trial. The special case where the first price is zero, the reference price you create is your own, and standard WTP instruments anchored on zero produce nonsense.
  8. What pricing signals. The quality-signal channel that breaks the monotone demand assumption, and how to reason about a price that is doing communication work as well as revenue work.
  9. AI cost-to-serve and pricing. The other half of the Gitavani analysis: stochastic, account-specific unit costs, how to model the distribution rather than the mean, and what a falling input-cost curve does to a price you have already signed.

Madad Clinic Cloud: Pricing Kalam Scribe

A teaching case on willingness-to-pay research

1. Opening

On the morning of Monday, 5 October 2026, Kiran Joshi sat in the Pune office of Madad Clinic Cloud with two spreadsheets open and a deadline that would not move. The company's board would meet on Friday, 9 October, and Kiran, its head of product, had to arrive with a single recommendation: what to charge for Kalam Scribe, a new artificial-intelligence assistant that listens to a doctor's consultation and drafts the prescription and notes. Launch was fixed for 26 October, ahead of Diwali on 8 November.

The chief executive, Meenakshi Raghavan, wanted a price the September survey could support, not one copied from a competitor or defended by instinct.

2. Company background

Madad Clinic Cloud was founded in Hyderabad in 2018 by two former hospital-software engineers. The company sells cloud software for independent doctors and small clinics: appointment booking, a digital prescription pad, billing, and patient reminders on WhatsApp. Its subscription, Madad Pro, costs ₹599 per doctor per month, excluding 18 per cent GST, and is collected through UPI autopay mandates.

By September 2026 about 40,000 doctors paid for Madad Pro. At that base, subscription revenue came to ₹239.60 lakh a month, or roughly ₹28.75 crore annualised. About 25,000 of those doctors practised alone; the remaining 15,000 worked in group clinics of two to six doctors.

The market was crowded and the neighbours were large. Practo dominated patient discovery, Eka Care had built a strong records product around the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission run by the National Health Authority, and a long tail of local billing tools sold for under ₹300 a month. Every vendor was adding ABDM-compatible records and watching the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. None had yet shipped a reliable scribe that handled the code-mixed speech of an Indian consultation. Kalam Scribe did, after eight months of work.

3. The situation

Kalam Scribe was expensive to run. Every consultation was streamed through speech recognition and a large language model, and Kavita Nambiar, the data scientist in Toronto who had modelled the cost, put it at ₹0.30 per consultation. A doctor seeing about 20 patients a day for 25 days generated roughly 500 consultations a month, which meant ₹150 of inference cost for every doctor who switched the feature on.

Rather than guess, Kiran had commissioned a willingness-to-pay study in September. Between 14 and 25 September, 240 doctors, drawn from Madad's own customers and from a purchased list of non-customers, answered a short survey by WhatsApp link, after watching a two-minute demonstration. It combined two methods. The Van Westendorp questions asked each doctor at what monthly price the scribe would seem too cheap to trust, a bargain, getting expensive, and too expensive. The Gabor-Granger questions then offered five prices in turn and asked whether the doctor would buy at each. The sample held 150 solo practitioners and 90 doctors in group clinics, roughly the mix of the customer base.

Exhibit 1 shows the Van Westendorp results. Exhibit 2 shows the Gabor-Granger acceptance counts. Exhibit 3 turns both into revenue for the installed base of 40,000 doctors. Prices throughout are per doctor per month, before GST.

The results did not point to one price. Solo practitioners found ₹449 the optimal price and thought anything above ₹749 too expensive. Group clinics put their optimal price at ₹699, and the pooled range that both groups tolerated stretched from ₹399 to ₹899. Group doctors judged ₹499 to be nearly too cheap, since their marginal cheapness point was ₹549. For a scribe writing medical notes, some explained, a low price felt like a warning.

Team members read the numbers through their own markets. Krish Venkatesh, the customer-success lead in Singapore, who spoke daily with small-town doctors that haggled over ₹100, worried that a solo doctor in Nagpur who felt overcharged in the first month would quietly cancel Madad Pro itself. Maitreyi Das, the designer in Berlin, had a different concern: she was building the pricing page and warned that two prices needed two clear names.

4. The people

Meenakshi Raghavan, chief executive, Hyderabad. She wanted the launch to lift revenue per doctor and protect gross margin ahead of the next fundraise.

Mohit Agarwal, sales head, New Jersey. Mohit sold Madad to hospital groups and diaspora-owned clinic chains, and he wanted one price on one page. Every extra tier, he said, added a week to a negotiation.

Kavita Nambiar, data scientist, Toronto. She wanted the team to remember what the survey could not say: stated intent overstates purchase, and doctors who had seen a demonstration were likelier to say yes than doctors who had not.

Krish Venkatesh, customer success, Singapore. He wanted the solo doctor protected, since solo doctors were 25,000 of the 40,000 paying customers and the most price-sensitive.

5. Exhibit 3 and the options

6. Questions for discussion

1. What does each Van Westendorp point in Exhibit 1 tell Kiran, and why does the pooled row hide more than it reveals?

2. Why is the revenue curve in Exhibit 2 nearly flat between ₹499 and ₹699, and what does the segment split show that the pooled figures do not?

3. Using Exhibit 3, compare the three options on adoption and contribution, and identify which non-financial risk each option carries.

4. Which option would you take to the board on Friday, and what evidence would you promise to collect after launch?

7. A note for the learner

How the topic frames the decision. Willingness-to-pay research does not deliver a price. It bounds one. Van Westendorp marks the zone in which a buyer will neither dismiss the product as cheap nor reject it as dear, and Gabor-Granger converts that zone into a demand curve and a revenue peak. Neither method sees cost, so the price must then be checked against unit economics, which for an AI feature means inference cost. A well-reasoned answer moves through those three steps in order: bound, choose, then check the margin.

One defensible path. Choose Option C. The pooled data suggests that ₹499 and ₹699 are equivalent, but that conclusion is an artefact of averaging two segments that value the scribe differently. Solo doctors tolerate up to ₹749 but prefer ₹449; group clinics distrust anything below ₹549 and are content at ₹699. Pricing each segment inside its own range yields ₹110.74 lakh of monthly contribution, the highest of the three options, with 26,000 doctors attaching. Option A gives up contribution and signals low quality to group buyers; Option B loses 6,000 attaching doctors and risks churn in the core plan.

The path has honest limits. Survey intent overstates purchase, so the attach rates in Exhibit 3 are ceilings, not forecasts. Mohit's negotiation concern is real and is best met by naming the tiers by clinic type rather than by price, and by making the group tier a per-doctor price that does not vary by hospital. Kiran should ask the board to approve the two prices as launch prices, then run a six-week live price test around ₹699 for group clinics, the segment with the least data. That is the step this topic unlocks: price testing inside the bounds the research set.
