Willingness-to-Pay Research: Bounding a Price You Can Defend

Van Westendorp, Gabor-Granger and conjoint analysis do not tell you what to charge. They tell you the range within which a price is defensible — and where in that range the arithmetic works in your favour.

1. A number on a slide, and a board meeting in three weeks

On the second Tuesday of April 2026, Ananya Rao, VP of Product at Velaan Health Systems, a Bengaluru-based maker of revenue-cycle-management software for mid-size Indian hospitals, sat in a glass-walled conference room with a single number on the whiteboard: ₹150. It was the price per bed per month that the sales team wanted to charge for Claims Guard, a new module that used a machine-learning model to flag insurance claims likely to be denied before the hospital submitted them — a problem that, across Velaan's 61 existing hospital customers, was quietly costing each facility between ₹9 lakh and ₹40 lakh a year in rejected TPA and insurer claims that were never resubmitted in time. The engineering lead had written a different number on the same board: ₹40, the fully loaded monthly cost of the GPU inference calls per bed at the volumes they expected. Between those two numbers sat the actual question, and nobody in the room could answer it with anything more than an opinion: what would a hospital administrator actually pay for this, and how much of that gap between ₹40 and ₹150 was margin Velaan was leaving on the table, versus margin that did not exist because no hospital would sign at ₹150 in the first place.

The stakes were not abstract. Velaan's annual user conference, where Claims Guard would be launched to all 61 existing accounts plus roughly 30 prospects in the pipeline, was ten weeks away. The CFO wanted the module paying back its own build cost within two quarters of general availability. The sales team, working from a handful of enthusiastic conversations with friendly hospital administrators during the beta, believed almost any price under ₹200 would sell. Ananya had seen this movie before: a launch price picked from confidence rather than evidence, followed six months later by an awkward renegotiation when adoption came in at a third of the forecast, or worse, a price so timid that hospitals happily paid it while Velaan quietly subsidised every claim it processed. She needed a number she could defend in front of the board, to the CFO, and to herself — not a guess dressed up as a decision.

2. The idea: replacing an unanswerable question with several answerable ones

Willingness-to-pay (WTP) research is the discipline of estimating, with some rigour, the maximum price a defined group of customers will pay for a defined offer — without ever asking them the one question that seems most direct and is, in fact, almost useless: "how much would you pay for this?" Ask that question and most respondents either lowball it strategically, hoping to influence the eventual price, or genuinely do not know, because nobody has ever asked them to put a number on something before they have had to write a cheque for it. WTP research was invented precisely to route around this failure. Instead of one unanswerable question, it asks a structured battery of answerable ones — about what feels cheap, what feels expensive, whether they would buy at a stated price, or which of two bundled offers they prefer — and then infers the price band from the pattern of those answers, the same way a doctor infers a diagnosis from several individually inconclusive symptoms rather than asking the patient to self-diagnose.

The two oldest and most widely taught methods are the Van Westendorp Price Sensitivity Meter, developed by the Dutch economist Peter van Westendorp in 1976 while working in market research in the Netherlands, and the Gabor-Granger method, published a decade earlier in 1966 by André Gabor and Clive Granger — the same Granger who would later share the 2003 Nobel Prize in Economics for work on time-series econometrics — while both were at the University of Nottingham. Conjoint analysis is older still in its mathematical roots, drawing on measurement theory published by Duncan Luce and John Tukey in 1964, but it was brought into marketing practice in the early 1970s by Paul Green, working with (among others) the Indian-American marketing scientist Vithala Rao, whose papers on conjoint measurement remain standard citations in every doctoral marketing syllabus that touches pricing, including at ISB. All three methods predate the modern SaaS pricing conversation by decades; what has changed is the ease of running them, not the logic underneath them.

The single sentence Ananya could repeat in a board meeting without sounding glib: "Willingness-to-pay research replaces the question customers cannot honestly answer with several they can, and triangulates a defensible price band from the pattern of their answers — it narrows uncertainty, it does not eliminate it."

That last clause matters more than it sounds. None of these three methods produces a single, unimpeachable "correct price." Each produces an estimate built on a stated preference, not an observed transaction, and stated preference is always vulnerable to the gap between what a respondent says in a ten-minute survey and what the same person does three months later staring at an actual invoice. The discipline is not in picking a method and trusting its output uncritically; it is in choosing the method that matches the decision at hand, running it on the right people, and treating convergence across two or three methods — not any single number — as the signal worth acting on.

3. How the three methods actually work, run one after another

Velaan did not pick one method. Ananya ran all three in sequence, because each answers a slightly different question and each compensates for a specific weakness in the one before it. The Van Westendorp Price Sensitivity Meter answers "within what range is a price acceptable at all, for this concept, described in general terms, with no other feature or bundle to react to?" It works by asking four questions about the same undescribed offer: at what price would this be so cheap you would question its quality ("too cheap")? At what price does it start to feel like a bargain ("cheap")? At what price does it start to feel expensive but you would still consider it ("expensive")? At what price is it so expensive you would not consider it at all ("too expensive")? Each respondent gives four numbers, in ascending order by construction. Plot the cumulative percentage of respondents whose threshold falls at or below each price, for all four questions, and you get four curves — two falling (too cheap, cheap) and two rising (expensive, too expensive) — whose crossing points bound the range of acceptable prices.

Gabor-Granger answers a narrower and more decision-useful question: "at this specific, named price, would you buy?" Respondents are shown a single price — sometimes ascending, sometimes descending, sometimes randomised to reduce anchoring — and asked for purchase intent on a scale (definitely would buy, probably would buy, probably would not, definitely would not). Repeat across five or six candidate prices and you can plot a demand curve: percentage who would buy, against price. Multiply price by that percentage at each point and you get a revenue index, and the price at which that index peaks is the Gabor-Granger estimate of the revenue-maximising price — a genuinely different output from Van Westendorp's range, because it optimises for revenue rather than simply asking what is tolerable.

Conjoint analysis answers the question neither of the first two methods can: "how much of what customers will pay is being driven by the price itself, and how much by the features bundled with it?" Respondents are shown several complete product profiles — each a specific combination of feature levels and a price — and asked to choose or rank them, never to react to price alone. Because price is varied independently of the feature levels across the profiles shown, a regression on the choices recovers a part-worth utility for each level of each attribute, including each price point, and those part-worths can be converted into a willingness-to-pay premium for any given feature. This is the method the topic's own curriculum note calls the strongest of the three, precisely because it is the only one that untangles price sensitivity from feature preference — a distinction that matters enormously the moment a company is deciding not just a price, but a bundle.

The step practitioners most often skip, at every one of these three stages, is screening the sample down to the actual economic buyer. A hospital's nursing staff will answer a survey about Claims Guard eagerly and inaccurately, because they do not sign the purchase order and have no sense of the hospital's software budget; the CFO or the procurement head does, and is the only respondent whose stated price threshold is worth plotting. Velaan's research vendor, an independent firm called Vezra Insights that Ananya retained for the study, insisted on this screen before fielding a single question, and it eliminated eleven of the fifty-four hospital contacts Velaan had originally proposed.

Figure 1. Three methods, three different questions, run in sequence: a qualitative probe narrows to a range (Van Westendorp), a point estimate sharpens that range against real revenue (Gabor-Granger), and conjoint separates the price signal from the feature signal before the company commits to live price testing.

4. The worked example: forty-three hospital administrators and three sets of arithmetic

Vezra Insights fielded the Van Westendorp questions to 43 screened economic buyers — CFOs, procurement heads, or, at smaller hospitals, the administrator who also held the purchasing mandate — drawn across Velaan's customer and prospect base. Table 1 shows the cumulative percentages built from their answers at twelve candidate monthly prices per bed, running from ₹60 to ₹400. Four crossing points matter, each with a name. The point of marginal cheapness (PMC) is where the "too cheap" and "expensive" curves cross — below it, more people think the price suspiciously low than think it expensive. Reading the table, at ₹150 too-cheap (42) still exceeds expensive (22), a gap of 20 points; by ₹180 expensive (38) has overtaken too-cheap (28), a gap of −10. Interpolating linearly between the two rows, the crossing falls 20/(20+10) = two-thirds of the way from ₹150 to ₹180, at roughly ₹170. The point of marginal expensiveness (PME) is where "cheap" and "too expensive" cross: at ₹210 cheap (44) exceeds too-expensive (20) by 24 points, and by ₹240 too-expensive (34) has overtaken cheap (29), a gap of −5; interpolating gives roughly ₹235. Between those two points sits the indifference price point (IPP), where "cheap" and "expensive" cross — between ₹180 (cheap 60, expensive 38, gap 22) and ₹210 (cheap 44, expensive 55, gap −11), interpolating to roughly ₹200 — and the optimal price point (OPP), where "too cheap" and "too expensive" cross, landing close by at roughly ₹205.

Ananya then ran the second pass the CFO had asked for: what does this range look like if she restricts the sample to hospitals under 200 beds, which tend to run tighter software budgets and had been the loudest voices in the beta pushing back on price? Re-running the same four questions on just those eighteen respondents shifted every curve down and to the left — the too-cheap curve now crossed the expensive curve near ₹115 instead of ₹170, and the cheap/too-expensive crossing fell near ₹165 instead of ₹235. The whole acceptable band for smaller hospitals compressed to roughly ₹115–₹165, a full ₹70–₹100 below the band for hospitals above 200 beds. That single re-cut of the same data was, in effect, the moment the pricing decision stopped being "what is the price" and became "how many prices," because a single number could not sit inside both bands without either overcharging the large hospitals' comfort zone or underpricing what large hospitals had already shown they would pay.

What made this second method valuable was not that it produced a sharper number than Van Westendorp; it was that it arrived at essentially the same number, ₹200, by an entirely different question and a different piece of arithmetic. Two independent methods converging on the same figure is a far stronger basis for a board slide than either method alone, precisely because the biases that distort stated purchase intent (a respondent wanting to seem like a savvy, price-sensitive buyer) are different from the biases that distort a too-cheap/too-expensive judgment (a respondent anchoring on what similar software "should" cost). If both biases were pulling the estimate the same direction, convergence would prove nothing; because they plausibly pull in different directions, convergence is evidence.

Conjoint: separating the price from the feature

The remaining open question was how much of that ₹200 was riding on a specific promise Velaan had been making informally in sales conversations — that Claims Guard's denial-prediction model ran at 95% accuracy — versus how much hospitals would pay for a materially cheaper 85%-accuracy version with a slower, batch turnaround instead of real-time flagging. Vezra ran a conjoint exercise on the same panel, showing each respondent a series of complete profiles combining three attributes — prediction accuracy (85% vs. 95%), turnaround (nightly batch vs. real-time), and price (₹150, ₹200, ₹250, ₹300) — and asked them to choose their preferred profile from each set. 5. Eight things a learner must get straight before trusting any of this

Stated intent is not observed behaviour

Every number above came from someone answering a survey question, not from someone signing a contract. Decades of replication in both consumer and B2B research show that stated purchase intent systematically overstates actual purchase — respondents are more generous in a low-stakes hypothetical than they will be with real budget on the line. Treat every WTP number as an upper bound on real demand, not a forecast of it, and discount accordingly when converting to a revenue plan.

The methods answer different questions, not the same question three ways

It is tempting to think of Van Westendorp, Gabor-Granger and conjoint as three ways of measuring the same underlying "true price." They are not. Van Westendorp measures acceptability of an undescribed concept; Gabor-Granger measures purchase intent at a named price for that same undescribed concept; conjoint measures trade-offs among fully specified bundles. Convergence between them is reassuring precisely because they are structurally different questions, not because they are redundant checks of the same one.

Willingness to pay is not a synonym for ability to pay

A hospital's finance head can sincerely believe Claims Guard is worth ₹250 a bed and still be unable to approve the purchase order until the next fiscal year's capital-and-software budget is set. WTP research measures perceived value; it says nothing about procurement calendars, sign-off chains, or whether the money is actually available this quarter. A high WTP number with a long approval cycle behind it is not the same finding as a high WTP number attached to a buyer who can sign tomorrow.

The sample must be the economic buyer, not the enthusiast

A common and expensive error is surveying the people who are easiest to reach — friendly beta users, the nursing staff who love the product, the champions inside an account — rather than the person who actually authorises the spend. Enthusiasts overstate willingness to pay because they are not the ones reconciling it against a budget; the correct respondent is whoever signs, or directly influences, the purchase order.

Prices need an anchor the respondent already trusts

Indian hospital buyers, like most B2B buyers, do not evaluate a price point in a vacuum; they compare it, consciously or not, to something they already know the going rate for — per-bed SaaS modules they already licence, or the per-claim fees charged by third-party claims-scrubbing vendors. A Van Westendorp or Gabor-Granger study that offers price points wildly outside any comparison the respondent has ever encountered risks collecting numbers that reflect confusion rather than judgment. Good practice bounds the tested price range using real market comparables, and includes at least one point clearly too cheap and one clearly too expensive, so the true crossing points are interpolated rather than extrapolated.

A WTP ceiling is a snapshot, not a constant

The range Velaan measured in April 2026 describes the market as it existed with no serious Indian competitor offering an AI denial predictor. If a competitor launches a comparable module within a year — and in Indian health-tech, that clock runs fast — the acceptable range will move, almost certainly downward, and the study will need repeating. Treat a WTP study as dated the moment it is filed, not as a permanent input.

None of these methods validates the business model

Even a perfectly executed WTP study answers only "what price is acceptable to charge," not "is this a good business at that price." It says nothing about churn, the cost of the sales motion required to close each deal, or whether ₹200 a bed at Velaan's actual GPU inference cost curve produces a defensible gross margin once support and onboarding are loaded in. WTP research is an input to a pricing decision, never a substitute for the unit-economics model that decision has to survive inside.

Order and framing effects are real and rarely disclosed

Whether Gabor-Granger prices are shown ascending, descending, or randomised changes the answers, because early prices anchor judgments of the ones that follow; whether a Van Westendorp question describes the concept generously or neutrally changes every threshold. A study report that does not disclose question order and concept framing should be treated with real suspicion, because the same underlying preferences can be made to produce noticeably different numbers by innocent-looking changes in survey design.

6. How the picture changes by business type and company stage

In consumer products, Van Westendorp remains the workhorse because large, low-cost samples are easy to gather online, and a single acceptable range per persona is often sufficient to set a shelf or subscription price without further segmentation. In B2B software like Velaan's, sample sizes are necessarily small — dozens, not thousands — which makes respondent screening far more consequential than sample size, and it is common to blend a formal method with real sales-led testing: a salesperson genuinely quoting a candidate price during a live deal and observing whether the prospect signs, which is closer to Gabor-Granger run with real stakes than to a survey. In marketplace and platform businesses, WTP research has to run on both sides of the transaction simultaneously, because a price change for buyers changes the supply sellers are willing to offer, and vice versa; the pricing lever under study is often a take rate or a listing fee rather than a sticker price, and conjoint is frequently used to test entire fee structures — flat fee versus percentage versus freemium-with-upsell — rather than a single number. Early-stage companies, with only a handful of paying customers, rarely have the sample size for a rigorous conjoint study and instead formalise the qualitative WTP probes built into early customer interviews, often backed by a small number of real paid pilots at varying prices; large, established companies like Velaan can run all three methods properly and then go further, testing live prices on real customer segments once the base is large enough to support a controlled experiment — the "price testing" this topic unlocks in the curriculum.

7. Common mistakes, and the cheapest way to catch each one

The survivorship-sample mistake. Symptom: the sales team reports that "everyone loves the price," a launch price is set high on that confidence, and adoption disappoints. Underlying error: the sample was built from happy existing customers and enthusiastic beta users, never from prospects who walked away or accounts that churned. Cheapest diagnostic: before trusting any WTP number, check whether lost deals and lapsed accounts were represented in the sample; if not, the number is a survivorship statistic, not a market estimate.

The narrow price-band mistake. Symptom: a conjoint or Gabor-Granger study returns a WTP figure that looks implausibly high relative to any comparable product on the market. Underlying error: the tested price range never included a point clearly too cheap or too expensive, so respondents were extrapolating preferences outside any range they actually evaluated, and the model's estimate is unreliable outside its tested bounds. Cheapest diagnostic: check whether the tested range bracketed the eventual estimate with genuine room on both sides; if the estimate sits at or beyond the edge of the tested range, distrust it.

The hypothetical-bias mistake. Symptom: the "optimal" price predicted from a WTP study is set at launch, and actual close rates come in well below the survey's predicted purchase intent. Underlying error: nobody discounted stated intent for the well-documented gap between hypothetical and real purchase behaviour. Cheapest diagnostic: before finalising a launch price from survey data alone, run a small live pilot — even ten real invoices at the candidate price — and compare actual close rates against the survey's predicted rate; the gap becomes the calibration factor for the next study.

The single-number mistake. Symptom: a pricing deck presents one number, with no range and no method disclosed, as though it were measured rather than estimated. Underlying error: treating a stated-preference estimate as a physical constant rather than a band with real uncertainty around it. Cheapest diagnostic: ask whoever built the number which two methods it was cross-checked against; if the honest answer is "none," the number deserves less confidence than the deck implies.

8. What good looks like

What Velaan actually did was, in miniature, what good WTP practice looks like everywhere: it ran two structurally different stated-preference methods and found they converged on the same figure before trusting either one; it used a third method to check whether that figure was a genuine price ceiling or an artefact of a specific feature promise; it deliberately re-cut the sample by an obvious segmentation variable (bed count) before assuming one price fit the whole customer base; it screened respondents down to the actual economic buyer rather than accepting whoever answered the phone; and it treated every output as an input to a margin and adoption model, not as the decision itself. None of that required exotic statistics — a spreadsheet, three surveys, and the discipline to distrust any single number were enough.

9. What Ananya decided, and what to learn next

Ananya set Claims Guard's base price at ₹199 per bed per month for the 85%-accuracy, nightly-batch tier, and ₹235 for a "Claims Guard Pro" tier running the 95%-accuracy real-time model — a structure the conjoint study justified almost to the rupee, and a base price sitting exactly where the Van Westendorp and Gabor-Granger studies had independently converged. For hospitals under 200 beds, she approved a lower entry price of ₹149, inside the narrower band that segment's own Van Westendorp curves had revealed, rather than forcing one national price onto a segment that had shown it would not accept it. Against the ₹40 GPU inference cost per bed, the base tier still cleared a healthy contribution margin even before onboarding and support costs, and the CFO signed off on the two-quarter payback target using ₹199 as the planning number, with ₹149 modelled explicitly as a lower-margin, higher-volume line rather than folded invisibly into a single blended average.

What she flagged for herself to learn next was price testing itself — the topic this one unlocks. Every number in this analysis was still a stated preference, gathered before a single hospital had paid a real invoice for Claims Guard; the genuinely rigorous next step, available to Velaan precisely because its installed base was large enough to support it, was a live experiment at general availability — offering different segments of new prospects genuinely different prices and observing actual close rates, the only data that settles the hypothetical-bias question this chapter kept raising but could not resolve on its own.

Two questions worth sitting with.

If the only WTP evidence you had were a single number that customers said they would pay in a friendly interview, how would you tell whether it reflected genuine value or simply the answer that felt safe to give the person asking?

When a company changes its price and its feature bundle at the same time — as most real launches do — can any WTP method, however carefully run beforehand, actually tell you afterward which of the two changes did the persuading?
